newsitem.title: INDIA: India gropes for new leader.
newsitem.headline: India gropes for new leader.

text.p: India's United Front alliance on Friday struggled to choose a new prime minister as renewed tension with its ally-turned-foe, the Congress party, threatened to delay an end to the nation's three-week political crisis.

Leaders of caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 15-party centre-left coalition gathered early on Friday ahead of a crucial meeting set for later in the day to try to select a new prime minister.
Nagging differences with Congress, political infighting and the death of a political boss prevented the United Front from meeting its own timetable and choosing a new leader on Thursday.
Parliament ended Deve Gowda's 10-month stint in power on April 11 when it voted by a lopsided margin against his government in a confidence motion.

Congress triggered his downfall when it withdrew its support on March 30. A day later, India's oldest party, which has ruled for all but four years since independence in 1947, staked a formal claim to power in a letter to the president.
But since the vote of confidence toppling Deve Gowda, the United Front and Congress have tried to sink their differences.
Congress has said it will back a new United Front coalition government provided the alliance replaces Deve Gowda as leader.

Deve Gowda has offered to step down. But left-wing parties in the United Front have insisted that Congress withdraw its March 31 letter to the president staking a claim to power before the alliance names a new leader.
Congress has told the front it has no designs on power but will revoke the letter only when a new leader is chosen.
In a sign of mounting anxiety over the impasse, the president met leaders of the three main formations on Thursday.
Sharma received Congress president Sitaram Kesri, Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Atal Behari Vajpayee and Communist Party of India-Marxist leader Harkishan Singh Surjeet.
But on Friday Kesri withdrew his request to stake a claim to power, according to Andhra Pradesh chief minister Chandrababu Naidu.

Newspapers said Sharma told the leaders that he wanted an end to the crisis by next Monday, when parliament was scheduled to sit in special session to take up the 1997/98 (April-March) budget, until now held hostage by the impasse.
Usually little more than a figurehead, the president holds the crucial authority in a crisis to name a new prime minister or dissolve the assembly and call elections.
Neither the United Front nor Congress wants snap polls which could catapult their common foe, the Hindu nationalist BJP, into power.

The right-wing BJP, however, has argued that the president should not ask the United Front to form the next government as it was thrown out of power last week. The Hindu nationalists would prefer the president to call elections.
The United Front's efforts were complicated by jockeying among candidates, which exposed splits within the coalition.

Regional parties were backing G.K. Moopanar, a former Congress member who defected last year to form a party in the southern state of Tamil Nadu. But members of Deve Gowda's Janata Dal were reluctant to relinquish power to regional allies.

The death of Janata Dal leader Bijoyananda Patnaik on Thursday also delayed efforts to solve the crisis. Deve Gowda and other United Front leaders were scheduled to attend his funeral in eastern India later on Friday.

The United Front's decision-making Steering Committee was scheduled to meet at 9:30 p.m. (1600 GMT). Asked if a new leader would be chosen on Friday, an aide to a senior United Front member said: "Most probably."
